explanations.explanation: Teaching it is. Jesus didn't want anyone to know because He was teaching His disciples. So this walk through Galilee was a classroom with no desks and no crowd. Just a teacher and His students on a quiet road.

Guarding sounds like a bodyguard situation, I get it. But the text never says Jesus was guarding anyone. It says He did not want anyone to know "because He was teaching His disciples." Teacher and students, that's the whole setup.

Sending would make this a trip with a to-do list and a few errands. But the text doesn't say Jesus was sending anyone anywhere here. It says He was teaching His disciples. That's the reason He kept things quiet.

Right. Jesus says the Son of Man will be delivered into the hands of men, and "They will kill Him…" He doesn't dress it up or soften it. That is a heavy thing to say on a walk, and I think it's why He wasn't done talking yet.
A crown would make a nicer headline, friend. But Jesus doesn't say that. He says, "They will kill Him…" Plain words, and no crown anywhere in that sentence.

Driven out is a fair guess, since people get pushed out of places all the time. But that's not what Jesus says. He says the men will kill Him, and then He adds that He will rise. Two very different endings, and He names both.
Three days. Jesus says, "…and after three days He will rise." That's the hopeful part of a very heavy sentence. He tells them both halves.
Seven is a nice, tidy number, I'll give you that. But Jesus says three, not seven. "…and after three days He will rise." Four days is a long time to wait for something He never said.
Forty is a big number, and it feels like it should be in there somewhere. But Jesus says three. "…and after three days He will rise." Short wait, huge promise.

The first half checks out. They did not understand what Jesus said. But the second half sneaks in something the text doesn't say. They were "…afraid to ask Him about it." So nobody asked, and nobody got an explanation right then.

False. They did not understand, and "…they were afraid to ask Him about it." Nobody raised a hand. I think we've all nodded along in a meeting at something we didn't get, then Googled it in the parking lot.
That's not how it went. Jesus asks what they were discussing, and the very next thing the text says is that they were silent. No quick answer came. Nobody even tried to change the subject.
False. Jesus asks the question, and the text says they were silent. Not one disciple jumped in. I bet you could've heard a cookie crumb land in that house.

explanations.answer: Which of them was the greatest
explanations.explanation: Yes. They had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. Twelve men, one question, and zero volunteers to repeat it to Jesus. When a whole room goes quiet like that, I think they already knew what He'd say.

explanations.answer: Why they couldn't drive out the spirit
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd guess that, since the spirit was just before this. But the text never says they argued about it. It says that on the way they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest.

explanations.answer: Who would carry the money bag
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a real argument a group could have. But the text doesn't mention a money bag here at all. It says they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest.

Last. Jesus says, "If anyone wants to be first, he must be the last of all and the servant of all." They were busy arguing about who's on top, and He turned the whole ladder upside down. Servant of all is the job description here.
Wisest sounds like a fair way to earn the top spot. But that's not what Jesus says. He says the one who wants to be first must be "the last of all and the servant of all." Last, not smartest.
Bravest sounds like it comes with a medal, friend. But Jesus says the one who wants to be first must be the last of all and the servant of all. A servant carries the tray, not the trophy.

explanations.answer: Takes the child in His arms
explanations.explanation: That's it. He has a little child stand among them, and then He takes the child in His arms. The disciples had been arguing about who's greatest, and now they're watching Jesus hold a child. Then He tells them about welcoming one.
Outside would be the opposite of the point. The text says Jesus had the child stand among them, then took the child in His arms. The child stays right there in the middle of the Twelve.
No question for the child here. Jesus has the child stand among them and takes the child in His arms. Then He speaks to the disciples, not to the child.
True. Jesus says, "…whoever welcomes Me welcomes not only Me, but the One who sent Me." So a welcome that starts small goes a long way up. That's a lot of weight on one little welcome.
It's actually true. Jesus says, "…whoever welcomes Me welcomes not only Me, but the One who sent Me." That means the welcome reaches the One who sent Him. Nothing in that line gets cut short.
True. John, one of the disciples, tells Jesus, "…we tried to stop him…" He says it right out loud. That's a brave thing to admit to the Teacher.
False. John, one of the disciples, says, "…we tried to stop him…" They didn't just watch the man. They stepped in. And John tells Jesus so himself.
Yes. John says they tried to stop him "…because he does not accompany us." The man was driving out demons in Jesus' name, but he wasn't part of their group. In other words, he wasn't on their roster.

explanations.answer: He was one of the scribes
explanations.explanation: John never says that. His reason is that the man "does not accompany us." Nothing about the man's job, only that he wasn't traveling with them.
Where the man was from never comes up. John gives one reason: "…he does not accompany us." The problem was who he traveled with, not where he lived.

Jesus never says the man will join the Twelve. His reason is this: "…no one who performs a miracle in My name can turn around and speak evil of Me." So the man doesn't need a spot on the roster. He's already working in Jesus' name.
False. Jesus says nothing about the man joining the Twelve. He says, "Do not stop him," and then gives His reason: "…no one who performs a miracle in My name can turn around and speak evil of Me."

explanations.answer: Anyone who is not against them
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jesus says, "For whoever is not against us is for us." Short line, big door. The circle is wider than the disciples thought.

explanations.answer: Only those who travel with them
explanations.explanation: That sounds like the rule John was using, since the man did not accompany them. But Jesus doesn't say that. He says, "…whoever is not against us is for us."

explanations.answer: Only those chosen as the Twelve
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't draw the line there. He says, "For whoever is not against us is for us." The Twelve were a small group, and He says the circle is bigger than that.
Reward. Jesus says the one who gives that cup of water "…will never lose his reward." A cup of water is not a fancy gift, friend. No big platter, no ribbon, and the reward still stays.
Place is a good guess, but that's not the word Jesus uses. He says the one who gives the cup of water "…will never lose his reward." The reward is what stays safe.
I've lost my way in a parking garage before, so I know that one's real. But Jesus doesn't say way here. He says the one who gives a cup of water "…will never lose his reward."

True, and I think this one is serious. Jesus says if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Him to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea. He speaks plainly because the little ones matter to Him.

It's true, and it's a heavy line. Jesus says it would be better for that person to have a large millstone hung around his neck and be thrown into the sea. That is how seriously He takes causing one of these little ones who believe in Him to stumble.
Eye. Jesus goes hand, then foot, then eye: "…if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out." Three warnings in a row, same serious tone. He doesn't soften any of them.
Tongue seems like a natural next one, but Jesus doesn't list it here. He goes from the hand to the foot, and then to the eye. "…if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out."
Heart is a good guess, since so much of life starts there. But in this passage Jesus names the hand, then the foot, then the eye. "…if your eye causes you to sin, pluck it out."

The kingdom of God. Jesus says it is better "…to enter the kingdom of God with one eye than to have two eyes and be thrown into hell…" The point is where you end up, not what you're carrying in. This is a heavy part, so I'll just say it plainly.
That's a lovely place, but Jesus doesn't name it here. He says it's better "…to enter the kingdom of God with one eye…" The kingdom of God is where He says to go in.
Jesus doesn't point to the city of David in this passage. He says it's better "…to enter the kingdom of God with one eye…" Same serious tone, and one clear destination.
That's it. Jesus says, "Salt is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it?" Salt that isn't salty has no job left. And then He gives them something to do with salt.
Bitter is a creative guess, but Jesus doesn't say it. He says salt can lose its saltiness. "…with what will you season it?" is the question He leaves them with.

Washing away is a reasonable guess, but that's not what Jesus describes. He says, "…if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it?" The salt is still there, it just isn't salty anymore.
Salt. Jesus says, "Have salt among yourselves…" He just talked about salt that can lose its saltiness, so now He says to keep it. It's an instruction to the whole group.
Peace. Jesus ends with "…be at peace with one another." Remember, these are the same disciples who had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. His last word to them is peace.
Love is a lovely word, and I can see why you picked it. But it isn't the word Jesus uses here. He says to have salt among yourselves and to be at peace with one another.
At odds is a real phrase, and it fits the argument on the road pretty well. But Jesus says the opposite. He tells them to be at peace with one another, not at odds.
Faith is a good word, but it isn't the one in this line. Jesus says, "Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another." The two words He picks are salt and peace.
